steps: Hold one arm horizontally across your chest.

tip: Plural of “Night” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out, palm up.
Tap the fingertips of your bent dominant hand twice on the inside of your wrist.
tip: Plural of “Doctor” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: With your dominant index and middle fingers, draw a small cross on your upper arm.
tip: Plural of “Hospital” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make the letter T: a fist with your thumb poking up between your index and middle fingers.
Shake it side to side twice.
tip: Plural of “Bathroom” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend your thumb and pinky (the Y handshape).
Hold it to the side of your head like a phone receiver.
tip: Plural of “Phone” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in front of you as if gripping a steering wheel.
Turn them slightly.
tip: Plural of “Car” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Touch your fingertips together to form a roof peak.
Move both hands down and outward to form the walls.
tip: Plural of “House” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Clap your dominant open hand down onto your non-dominant open palm.
tip: Plural of “School” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make both hands into flat open hands, fingers together.
Press your palms together in front of your chest, fingertips pointing forward.
Open the hands outward twice, like swinging a book's covers open.
Keep your palms facing each other as the hands open.
Use the double motion for the noun BOOK; a single opening means OPEN-BOOK.
tip: Plural of “Book” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, like a page.
Form a V with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand, fingertips pinched together like two eyeballs.
Sweep the V fingertips down across the palm, from wrist toward fingers.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingertips glide.
A single sweep means READ; repeat the sweep to mean READING.
tip: “Reads” is signed with the base READ sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, like a page.
Form a V with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand, fingertips pinched together like two eyeballs.
Sweep the V fingertips down across the palm, from wrist toward fingers.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingertips glide.
A single sweep means READ; repeat the sweep to mean READING.
tip: “Reading” is signed with the base READ sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an H, index and middle fingers extended together.
Hold the H handshape in front of your chest, palm facing your non-dominant side.
Move the hand straight down twice in place, with a slightly extended wrist.
Keep both downward taps even and centered; do not drift sideways.
Hold a neutral expression — drifting to the side can read as HARD-OF-HEARING.
tip: Plural of “History” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into loose C handshapes, fingers curved.
Hold them in front of your chest with the palms facing each other.
Move both hands in a circle so the two C hands come together in the middle.
Finish with the hands nearly touching, palms still facing each other.
Keep the sweep smooth and symmetrical, like students gathering in a room.
tip: Plural of “Class” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into loose flat hands, palms facing down.
Hold your non-dominant hand steady as a base in front of your chest.
Circle your dominant hand once, then slap it down onto the base hand.
Keep both palms facing down as the dominant hand lands.
Let the hand bounce back up after the slap — freezing on the base reads wrong.
tip: Plural of “College” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up.
Pinch your dominant fingertips and thumb together just above the palm.
Lift the pinched fingers up toward your forehead, as if grabbing information.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while you lift.
Aim for the forehead itself, not the top of the head, to keep it LEARN and not TEACH.
tip: “Learns” is signed with the base LEARN sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up.
Pinch your dominant fingertips and thumb together just above the palm.
Lift the pinched fingers up toward your forehead, as if grabbing information.

tip: “Learning” is signed with the base LEARN sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up.
Pinch your dominant fingertips and thumb together just above the palm.
Lift the pinched fingers up toward your forehead, as if grabbing information.

Aim for the forehead itself, not the top of the head, to keep it LEARN and not TEACH.
tip: Past form of “Learn” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Make both hands into fists with the thumbs pointing straight up, like little beakers.
Hold your non-dominant fist steady in front of your chest.
Tip your dominant fist over it, as if pouring liquid from a test tube into the beaker.
Keep both thumbs pointing up through the pour.
Pair it with a curious, inquisitive expression — science is about wondering.
tip: Plural of “Science” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an L, index finger up and thumb out.
Hold the L handshape in front of your chest.
Draw a full circle in the air with the L handshape.
Trace the circle clockwise from your own point of view if you are right-handed.
Keep your face relaxed; mirror the direction if your local signers circle the other way.
tip: Plural of “Library” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend the index fingers of both hands, other fingers tucked.
Bend each index finger into an X hook while your hands move downward.
Trace a question mark in the air, then open both hands into palm-down fives to dot it.
Keep the movement centered in front of your chest.
Use this formal two-handed version for exams; casual quizzes are often just fingerspelled.
tip: Plural of “Test” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, like an open book.
Point the fingers of your dominant hand down at the palm.
Wiggle your dominant fingers as you hover over the page.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingers flutter.
Lean your head in a little to show concentration — STUDY is an active sign.
tip: “Studies” is signed with the base STUDY sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, like an open book.

Wiggle your dominant fingers as you hover over the page.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingers flutter.
Lean your head in a little to show concentration — STUDY is an active sign.
tip: “Studying” is signed with the base STUDY sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, and keep it low.
Pinch your dominant fingertips together over the palm and lift them toward your head.
Open both hands into flat palms facing inward.
Move both flat hands straight down past your torso to finish the PERSON ending.
Keep the non-dominant hand down — lifting it toward the head would read as TEACHER.
tip: Plural of “Student” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Bring your dominant flat hand down on top of it, palm to palm.
Strike the palm twice with a quick repeated backward bounce.
Keep your non-dominant hand perfectly still — only the dominant hand moves.
Two clean strikes is enough; extra hits make it look like you are fanning yourself.
tip: Plural of “Paper” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold up the index finger of your dominant hand, other fingers tucked.
Raise it in front of your chest, palm facing sideways.
Draw a question mark in the air: curve down, then finish with a quick X-hook dot.
Keep the curve and the dot in one smooth flowing motion.
Pair it with raised eyebrows and a slight forward lean — the classic questioning face.
tip: Plural of “Question” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, as your paper.
Pinch your dominant index fingertip against the dip of your thumb, like holding a pen.
Scribble a quick side-to-side motion across the palm.
Keep your dominant palm angled sideways while the pen hand moves.
One careful stroke means writing something specific, like your name; quick repeats mean writing in general.
tip: “Writes” is signed with the base WRITE sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant index finger up in front of your chest.
Shape your dominant hand into a G, index finger pointing sideways.
Touch the dominant G fingertip to the side of the non-dominant index finger.
Angle both palms inward toward each other.
Hold the touch for a beat so the word 'lands' before you move on.
tip: Plural of “Word” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Touch your dominant index fingertip to your lips.
Hold your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest.
Move both hands forward and slightly down together.
Close both hands into loose fists as they travel forward.
Finish with the fists facing each other at chest height, as if delivering a reply.
tip: “Answers” is signed with the base ANSWER sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Shape your dominant hand into a G, index and thumb pinched together.
Tap the G hand down onto the palm twice, bouncing down, up, then down again.
Point the dominant index finger toward your non-dominant side as you tap.
Two taps is the standard rhythm; more taps make it look like you are counting.
tip: Plural of “Grade” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into flattened O handshapes, fingertips touching thumbs.
Hold both hands up near your forehead.
Move both hands forward about six inches.
Change both hands into flat palms facing inward.
Sweep both flat hands straight down past your torso to finish the PERSON ending.
tip: Plural of “Teacher” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into F handshapes, thumb and index pinched into circles.
Hold your non-dominant F hand steady in front of your chest.
Circle your dominant F hand forward around it, tracing a dinner-table circle.
Bring both F hands together so the fingertips touch.
Keep the circle smooth — a jerky trace can read as a different group sign.
tip: Plural of “Family” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open your dominant hand with the fingers together pointing up.
Touch your thumb to your forehead, palm facing left.
Bring the hand straight down to your chest.
Finish with the thumb touching your chest, fingers still pointing up.
Keep the motion smooth and centered — starting at the chin instead would mean WOMAN.
tip: Plural of “Man” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in flat open handshapes, fingers together.
Raise them to the sides of your torso, palms facing inward.
Move both hands straight down past your body.
Keep the palms facing each other through the whole drop.
Hold a neutral face — PERSON is the plain citation form for an individual.
tip: Plural of “Person” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a 5, with your thumb sticking out to the side.
Touch the tip of your thumb to your chin, fingers pointing upward.
Bring the hand straight down until your thumb-tip rests on the center of your chest.
Keep your palm angled toward your face through the short downward slide.
Hold a neutral, respectful expression — this is the everyday adult-female sign.
tip: Plural of “Woman” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant forearm horizontally in front of you, as if cradling a baby.
Shape your dominant hand into a flat B, with the palm facing toward your left.
Touch the edge of the dominant hand to your forehead like a salute, marking the male part.
Sweep the dominant hand down into the crook of your non-dominant elbow, ending palm up.
Keep the cradled arm still — do not rock it side to side, that extra movement belongs to BABY.
tip: Plural of “Son” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a loose C, as if about to cup something small.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your chest with its palm facing up.
Start the C-hand at your chin to mark the female part of the compound.
Glide the C-hand down from your chin and settle it into the upturned palm.
Close the C gently around the lower hand, like two hands joining in marriage.
tip: Plural of “Wife” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands open with fingers spread and thumbs sticking out to the sides.
Touch both thumb-tips to your forehead, marking the father part of the compound.
Slide both hands straight down until the thumb-tips touch your chin for the mother part.
Keep your palms angled toward each other and your fingers relaxed through the slide.
Pair the slide with a small nod — you are naming a respected relationship.
tip: Plural of “Parent” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a flattened O, fingertips pinched together and facing you.
Bring your fingertips up to your mouth, as if placing a bite of food inside.
Tap your mouth twice with a small, repeated movement.
Keep your fingers relaxed and your wrist loose; the motion stays small and quick.
Nod slightly, as if enjoying the taste — eating is a pleasant sign.
tip: Plural of “Food” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist and bend your index finger into an X handshape.
Press the bent knuckle of your index finger firmly against your cheek.
Pivot your wrist to twist the knuckle back and forth on your cheek.
Keep your palm facing sideways and your elbow steady so only the wrist turns.
Imagine biting into a crisp apple — the twist mimics the chewing motion.
tip: Plural of “Apple” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, as if wrapping your fingers around a cup.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with its palm facing up.
Set the C-hand down into the upturned palm, like placing a cup on a saucer.
Add a very small repeated up-and-down motion — keep it tiny, not a big bounce.
Keep your expression neutral; you are showing an object, not drinking from it.
tip: Plural of “Cup” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into S fists, with your thumbs resting against the curled fingers.
Stack your dominant fist on top of your non-dominant fist in front of your chest.
Hold the bottom fist completely still, like the base of an old coffee grinder.
Turn the top fist in small circles, as if cranking the grinder's handle.
Keep your palms facing down and add a focused look — grinding takes effort.
tip: Plural of “Coffee” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand up near your side, shaped like a modified D.
Snap your middle finger against the base of your thumb, landing in a G-like shape.
Repeat the snap a second time in the same spot.
Keep your palm facing forward and make the snaps small and crisp.
Some signers pat their thigh first — that version is fine, but the snap is the core.
tip: Plural of “Dog” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands up with fingers extended and held straight together.
Touch your fingertips to the center of your chest.
Pivot both hands inward toward each other, then back out, repeating twice.
Keep your fingertips on your chest the whole time — the wrists do the work.
Breathe visibly as you sign, matching the rise and fall of an animal's chest.
tip: Plural of “Animal” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an H: index and middle fingers extended together, other fingers folded.
Hold the H-hand beside your head at temple height.
Bend the two fingers forward twice, like a horse's ears flicking.
Keep your palm facing forward and your elbow relaxed at your side.
Sign with one hand only — skilled signers do not use two hands for HORSE in conversation.
tip: Plural of “Horse” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand out to the side with fingers together and palm facing sideways.
Keep your wrist loose and your arm extended at a comfortable height.
Wave your hand side to side while gliding it forward a few inches.
Let the hand trail like a fish's tail — the wiggle comes from the wrist, not the elbow.
Keep a calm, smooth expression to match the gliding swim.
tip: Plural of “Fish” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an open F: thumb and index nearly touching, other fingers spread.
Hold the open F near the corner of your mouth.
Pull the hand outward to the side while closing the thumb and index into a full F.
Keep the outward pull short, about an inch or two, tracing the whisker line.
Imagine stroking a cat's whiskers — keep your face soft and playful.
tip: Plural of “Cat” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with its palm facing down.
Lay your dominant flat hand on the back of it, palm down.
Stroke forward along the back of the hand twice, like petting an animal's back.
Keep your dominant fingers together and make the strokes long and gentle.
Soften your expression — done gently, the sign doubles as the verb 'to pet'.
tip: Plural of “Pet” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand open with all five fingers spread.
Bring the open hand up in front of your mouth and chin.
Flutter your fingers up and down in a quick wiggle.
Keep your palm facing you and make the fluttering motion small and lively.
Raise your eyebrows slightly, as if asking about or showing off colors.
tip: Plural of “Color” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand open in a 5, with your middle finger aimed at your earlobe.
Bring the open hand up beside your ear, as if pointing at a gold earring.
Pull the hand downward, closing it into a Y handshape with thumb and pinky out.
Twist the Y once or twice as you pull it down past your cheek.
Keep the motion close to your cheek and finish with the Y pointing downward.
tip: Plural of “Gold” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Bend the middle finger of your dominant hand forward at the large knuckle, keeping the other fingers relaxed.
Place the bent middle fingertip against the center of your chest, slightly toward your dominant side.
Stroke the fingertip upward along your chest in one smooth motion, then repeat the stroke.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your chest for the whole movement.
Match your face to the feeling you mean, since this sign carries emotional meaning.
tip: “Feels” is signed with the base FEEL sign.

steps: Bend the middle finger of your dominant hand forward at the large knuckle, keeping the other fingers relaxed.
Place the bent middle fingertip against the center of your chest, slightly toward your dominant side.
Stroke the fingertip upward along your chest in one smooth motion, then repeat the stroke.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your chest for the whole movement.
Match your face to the feeling you mean, since this sign carries emotional meaning.
tip: “Feeling” is signed with the base FEEL sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a U, with the index and middle fingers extended together.
Hold your non-dominant hand in a fist at chest height as a steady base.
Bring the U-hand down so the fingers rest on the back or side of the base fist.
Turn the U-hand's palm sideways so the fingers point down onto the base hand.
Keep your body still and your expression neutral; this is a plain action verb.
tip: “Uses” is signed with the base USE sign.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a U, with the index and middle fingers extended together.
Hold your non-dominant hand in a fist at chest height as a steady base.
Bring the U-hand down so the fingers rest on the back or side of the base fist.
Turn the U-hand's palm sideways so the fingers point down onto the base hand.
Keep your body still and your expression neutral; this is a plain action verb.
tip: “Using” is signed with the base USE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a U, with the index and middle fingers extended together.
Hold your non-dominant hand in a fist at chest height as a steady base.
Bring the U-hand down so the fingers rest on the back or side of the base fist.
Turn the U-hand's palm sideways so the fingers point down onto the base hand.
Keep your body still and your expression neutral; this is a plain action verb.
tip: Past form of “Use” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Make a V with your dominant hand, extending your index and middle fingers together.
Start with the fingertips just below your eyes, pointing forward.
Move the V-hand straight outward away from your face toward what you see.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your own face during the movement.
Aim your eyes in the same direction as the movement to show what you are looking at.
tip: “Sees” is signed with the base SEE sign.

steps: Make a V with your dominant hand, extending your index and middle fingers together.
Start with the fingertips just below your eyes, pointing forward.
Move the V-hand straight outward away from your face toward what you see.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your own face during the movement.
Aim your eyes in the same direction as the movement to show what you are looking at.
tip: “Seeing” is signed with the base SEE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of you as loose open claws, fingers spread and slightly bent.
Start with your hands at arm's length, away from your torso.
Pull both hands back toward your body while closing each hand into a fist.
Turn your palms to face each other as your fists land near your chest.
Add a small nod or satisfied look, as if you have just received something.
tip: “Gets” is signed with the base GET sign.

Flick your middle finger upward twice so it thumps lightly against the underside of your chin.
Angle your palm toward your face with the flicking finger pointing up.
Keep the thump gentle — you barely need to touch your chin for it to read.
Hold a neutral expression; let the double flick do all the talking.
tip: Plural of “Light” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form a flattened O handshape with your dominant hand, your fingertips rounded and relaxed.
Hold the O up near the top of your head, like the sun overhead.
Circle the O hand once, then bring it down an inch or two as you open it wide.
Let your palm face down as the hand opens, spreading all your fingers.
Look up toward the hand as you sign, tracking the sun's descent.
tip: Plural of “Sun” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm down, like a bed of sand.
Hover your dominant hand above it with your fingers loose and slightly curved.
Wiggle your dominant fingers as the hand sweeps over the back of the base hand.
Let the pass suggest a wave splashing onto the shore and pulling back to the sea.
Keep a relaxed, happy expression and glance at your hands as the 'water' flows.
tip: Plural of “Beach” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form W handshapes with both hands: fold your pinky down with your thumb, three fingers up.
Raise both W hands to shoulder height, side by side.
Move both hands downward with a wavy, zigzag motion, like weather rolling in.
Keep both palms facing forward as your hands ripple downward.
Let the waviness flow through your wrists — stiff hands make it read wrong.
Hold a curious expression, as if checking the sky for what is coming.
tip: Plural of “Weather” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Raise your non-dominant index finger so it points straight up, like a candle.
Touch the top of that index finger with your dominant index fingertip.
Slide your dominant fingertip down the side of the index to its base.
Keep your dominant palm facing back toward you during the whole slide.
Repeat the downward slide a second time to mean monthly, as in a rent payment.
tip: Plural of “Month” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands open and relaxed at chest height, thumbs upright.
Poke the tips of both thumbs into your upper chest twice.
Angle your palms down and inward so both thumb tips reach your chest easily.
tip: Plural of “Holiday” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point your dominant index finger up, like the minute hand of a clock.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you as the clock face.
Circle your index finger once around the base hand, completing a full revolution.
tip: Plural of “Hour” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point your dominant index finger up in a 1 handshape.
Wipe the fingertip across your forehead from one temple to the other.
Close the hand into an X handshape as it crosses, like wiping away sweat.
tip: Plural of “Summer” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend your non-dominant arm forward as a tree branch, hand in a loose fist.
Raise your dominant hand open, palm down, beside your non-dominant elbow.
Brush the open hand downward past the elbow twice, like leaves dropping off the branch.
tip: Plural of “Fall” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a loose fist or sideways C at chest height.
Squeeze your dominant hand into a flat O, palm up, beneath the fist.
Push the squeezed hand up through the fist and open it into a 5 as it rises.
Repeat the rising bloom a second time to mark the season.
tip: Plural of “Spring” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form both hands into W handshapes and hold them at chest height.
Keep your palms facing each other as the two W hands tremble in place.
Shake both hands with a small, quick shivering motion, side to side.
tip: Plural of “Winter” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point your dominant index finger like the minute hand of a clock.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady in front of you as the clock face.
Tick the index fingertip forward a short distance across the base palm.
Drive the ticking from your wrist, keeping the finger itself still.
tip: Plural of “Minute” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form both hands into W handshapes, three fingers spread upright.
Stack your dominant W directly on top of your non-dominant W at chest height.
Circle both hands around each other — right hand forward, left hand back — like the earth orbiting.
Keep the orbiting smooth and continuous, ending where the hands started.
tip: Plural of “World” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Spread both hands into open fives with fingers wide apart in front of your torso.
Hold both hands at chest height with your palms turned to face you.
Push both hands upward in a flickering motion, raising and lowering them alternately.
Wiggle all ten fingers as the hands rise, like flames licking upward.
Keep your expression neutral; the quick finger wiggle sells the motion of fire.
tip: Plural of “Fire” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Tap the fingers of a W handshape against your chin to sign WATER first.
Hold both flat hands in neutral space with fingers pointing forward.
Turn both palms to face each other, about a foot apart.
Sweep both hands forward together in a curvy side-to-side zigzag.
Keep the zigzag smooth and continuous, picturing a winding stream flowing onward.
tip: Plural of “River” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands open and relaxed, fingers together and slightly spread.
Place both hands out in front of your waist, side by side.
Turn your palms down and let them face the floor.
Move both hands up and down in small rolling waves, pushing slightly forward.
Keep the two hands moving in sync, like twin swells rolling under them.
tip: Plural of “Sea” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Plant your non-dominant elbow near your waist and raise that forearm upright like a trunk.
Open your dominant hand into a five with fingers spread wide.
Rest the wrist of the open five on top of the upright forearm.
Twist the open hand left and right twice from the wrist.
Keep the forearm steady and upright so it reads as the tree trunk.
tip: Plural of “Tree” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into fists and tap your dominant fist on top of the other twice to sign ROCK.
Open both hands and raise them upward in front of your chest.
Stack the hands with one above the other, the higher hand near your forehead.
Turn both palms to face away from you as you lift.
Look up slightly as the hands rise, showing the great height of the peak.
tip: Plural of “Mountain” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form the sign for TREE: forearm upright as trunk, open five twisted twice on top.
Extend your non-dominant forearm horizontally in front of your chest.
Set the tree handshape near your wrist at the far end of that forearm.
Slide the tree handshape sideways along the top of the forearm to the elbow.
Keep your face relaxed; the repeated sliding tree tells the whole story.
tip: Plural of “Forest” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed fives with fingers slightly spread.
Hold the hands out in front of your shoulders, a foot apart.
Turn both palms to face each other across the gap.
Sweep both hands sideways together, then back, repeating the motion twice.
Puff your cheeks or blow gently to sell the breeze with your face.
tip: Plural of “Wind” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl both hands into stiff claws, fingers hooked and spread apart.
Hold the clawed hands in front of your chest, a few inches apart.
Pull both hands sharply inward toward your body in one quick jerk.
Turn both palms down as the hands snap back toward you.
Tense your shoulders and freeze your face, as if the cold has seized you.
tip: Plural of “Ice” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Touch the fingertips of your O handshape to the corner of your mouth.
This opening move borrows the EAT sign for where meals happen.
Slide the same O handshape upward to rest against your cheekbone.
The cheek touch borrows SLEEP, where rest happens each night.
Keep the motion smooth and unhurried, like settling into your own rooms.
tip: Plural of “Home” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat at waist height, palm facing up, like an open book.
Form an A fist with your dominant hand, thumb pressed against the knuckles.
Raise the dominant fist over the open hand and flick the thumb upward.
Sweep the raised thumb sideways across the open palm, as if flipping a page over.
Keep your gaze on the open hand, as if reading the page you just turned.
tip: Plural of “Page” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a C, thumb and fingers forming a claw.
Raise the C hand to the middle of your face, beside your nose.
Circle the C hand clockwise around the center of your face.
Turn the palm to face left (if right-handed) as the hand orbits.
Squint slightly or scan your eyes around, as if hunting for something.
tip: “Searches” is signed with the base SEARCH sign.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a C, thumb and fingers forming a claw.
Raise the C hand to the middle of your face, beside your nose.
Circle the C hand clockwise around the center of your face.
Turn the palm to face left (if right-handed) as the hand orbits.
Squint slightly or scan your eyes around, as if hunting for something.
tip: “Searching” is signed with the base SEARCH sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a C, thumb and fingers forming a claw.

Turn the palm to face left (if right-handed) as the hand orbits.
Squint slightly or scan your eyes around, as if hunting for something.
tip: Past form of “Search” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Form the letter W with your dominant hand, three fingers spread and thumb tucked.
Hold the W up at chest height in neutral space in front of you.
Produce the W handshape twice in quick succession, resetting between forms.
Turn your palm to face forward during each of the two Ws.
Keep your face neutral; this technical sign carries no special expression.
tip: Plural of “Site” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B handshapes, fingers pressed together and thumbs tucked across the palms.
Hold your non-dominant hand steady at chest height with its palm facing down as the base.
Lift your dominant hand with the palm facing outward, toward the side.
Stroke the dominant hand leftward across the top of the base hand so the two hands brush.
Sweep the dominant hand back rightward along the same path, keeping both hands flat.
Keep your face neutral; using an S-fist instead of a flat base hand is a common regional variant.
tip: Plural of “Business” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form the letter W with your dominant hand, spreading your index, middle, and ring fingers upright.
Hold the W at chest height with your palm facing forward.
Move the W through a small sideways arc while keeping the handshape fixed.
Form a second W at the end of the arc, pausing briefly on each letter.
Keep your expression neutral and let the smooth arc carry both letters as one flowing sign.
tip: Plural of “Web” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into D letters: index fingers pointing up, other fingers curled in a circle with the thumb.
Hold both hands at chest height with the fingertips aimed straight up.
Bring the two index fingertips together until they touch lightly.
Pull the hands an inch apart, then bring the fingertips together a second time.
Keep the double touch small and quick, like a light double-tap.
tip: Plural of “Date” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand upright at chest height, fingers pointing straight up.
Turn that hand's palm sideways, toward your midline, like a standing post.
Shape your dominant hand flat, fingers together, palm facing down.
Rest the flat hand level just above the fingertips of the upright hand.
Let the flat hand mark the highest point, like a roof sitting on a post.
tip: Plural of “Top” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand up at chest height, index and middle fingers extended together.
Extend the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand in the same shape.
Bring the dominant fingers down onto the matching fingers of the base hand.
Tap the base fingers twice with a small, firm double contact.
Keep both palms facing down or angled slightly sideways through the taps.
tip: Plural of “Name” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an S fist with your dominant hand, fingers curled and thumb across them.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat at chest height, palm up, as a steady base.
Touch the side of the S fist against the middle of the base palm.
Slide the S hand in a small arc down to the lower part of the base palm.
Keep the movement short and controlled, staying in touch with the base hand.
Keep your expression neutral — this is a plain vocabulary sign.
tip: Plural of “State” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a C, curving your fingers into a loose tunnel.
Hold the C hand at chest height with its opening facing sideways.
Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, tucking the other fingers away.
Thread the index fingertip straight through the tunnel of the C hand in one pass.
Use a single smooth pass for the verb; repeat the pass for the noun.
tip: Past form of “Email” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Open both hands into loose 5 handshapes, with all fingers comfortably spread apart.
Bend your non-dominant arm to about 45 degrees and hold it across your chest.
Place your dominant 5 hand just behind the non-dominant hand, above the forearm.
Wave the dominant hand back and forth above the arm in a steady rhythm.
Keep the dominant palm facing your chest while the hand waves side to side.
Keep a relaxed, pleasant expression, as if you are enjoying a favorite song.
tip: Plural of “Music” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make flat hands with both hands, keeping the fingers of each hand together.
Touch your fingertips together in front of your chest, forming a small rooftop shape.
Separate your hands slightly while sliding them sideways to a new spot.
Touch your fingertips together again once the hands reach the new position.
Angle both palms downward and toward each other, keeping the rooftop shape intact.
Keep your expression neutral and your shoulders still; the hands paint the skyline.
tip: Plural of “City” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an S handshape with both hands by closing each hand into a fist.
Hold your non-dominant fist steady at chest height in front of you.
Place your dominant fist just below the non-dominant fist to start.
Push the dominant fist upward until it meets the underside of the other fist.
Keep both palms facing toward you for the entire upward push.
Nod once with a sincere expression, showing that you stand behind someone.
tip: “Supports” is signed with the base SUPPORT sign.

steps: Make an S handshape with both hands by closing each hand into a fist.

Nod once with a sincere expression, showing that you stand behind someone.
tip: Past form of “Support” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Shape both hands into loose flat palms, keeping the fingers relaxed and together.
Hold your non-dominant hand steady in front of your chest as the base hand.
Circle your dominant hand above the base hand, then slap it downward and lift it back up a few inches.
Keep both palms facing down throughout the circling and slapping motion.
Keep your expression neutral; repeat the slap once or twice for a natural rhythm.
tip: Plural of “University” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Bend the fingers of your dominant hand into a loose claw shape.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm turned up.
Circle the bent fingertips once or twice above the open palm.
Drop the fingertips down to touch the middle of the upturned palm.
Keep your gaze and expression neutral; the sign marks one central spot.
tip: Plural of “Center” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an A fist with your dominant hand, thumb sticking up.
Raise the fist near your mouth, as if the thumb were a stamp you just licked.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you like an envelope.
Move the A fist down and press the thumb onto the flat palm.
Keep your expression neutral; the sign also covers a single piece of mail.
tip: Plural of “Mail” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Flatten both hands with the fingers together and extended.
Hold both hands apart in the lower space in front of your torso.
Move both hands forward once in a single smooth push.
Point the fingertips outward with both palms facing each other.
Keep your face neutral; the sign means a method or manner of doing something.
tip: Plural of “Way” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into "1" handshapes, extending only the index fingers while the thumbs fold across the palms.
Hold both hands out in front of your chest, with the index fingers angled comfortably at about 45 degrees.
Draw large circles in the air with the tips of your index fingers, moving both hands at the same time.
Circle both hands in the same direction, keeping one hand half a lap ahead of the other, like the hands of a clock.
Keep your face relaxed and neutral; you may pedal the circles forward or backward, but pick one direction.
tip: “Signs” is signed with the base SIGN sign.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an "S" fist, folding the fingers down over the thumb.
Hold the fist in front of your chest at a comfortable height, ready to move downward.
Move the whole fist straight downward in one short, smooth motion.
Keep the palm of the fist angled toward your non-dominant side; a palm-down variant is also widely used.
Keep your face neutral and let the downward drop be crisp and deliberate, like pointing at the bottom of a map.
tip: Plural of “South” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into "10" hands, making fists with the thumbs extended upward.
Hold both hands a bit apart in the space in front of your chest.
Tap the two hands toward each other twice, letting the thumbs briefly bump.
Keep the thumbs facing each other and the palms turned back toward you throughout the taps.
Keep your expression neutral and make the taps light and rhythmic, not forceful.
tip: Plural of “Game” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a clawed "5", spreading the fingers and bending them slightly.
Raise your non-dominant arm a little so the opposite upper arm becomes the target.
Bring the dominant hand down so the clawed fingertips land firmly on the opposite upper arm.
Keep the dominant palm angled down toward the arm as the fingertips strike.
Use a firm, confident expression and tense the shoulders slightly to show force.
tip: Plural of “Power” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into horizontal "V" hands, extending the index and middle fingers out sideways.
Stack the dominant "V" hand on top of the non-dominant "V" hand in front of your body.
Move both hands forward together in a small circular motion, repeating the circle twice.
Keep both "V" hands horizontal and stacked, with the fingertips pointing forward as they circle.
Keep a warm, gentle expression; this sign conveys watchful, attentive kindness.
tip: “Cares” is signed with the base CARE sign.

steps: Shape both hands into horizontal "V" hands, extending the index and middle fingers out sideways.
Stack the dominant "V" hand on top of the non-dominant "V" hand in front of your body.
Move both hands forward together in a small circular motion, repeating the circle twice.
Keep both "V" hands horizontal and stacked, with the fingertips pointing forward as they circle.
Keep a warm, gentle expression; this sign conveys watchful, attentive kindness.
tip: “Caring” is signed with the base CARE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Shape both hands into horizontal "V" hands, extending the index and middle fingers out sideways.
Stack the dominant "V" hand on top of the non-dominant "V" hand in front of your body.
Move both hands forward together in a small circular motion, repeating the circle twice.
Keep both "V" hands horizontal and stacked, with the fingertips pointing forward as they circle.
Keep a warm, gentle expression; this sign conveys watchful, attentive kindness.
tip: Past form of “Care” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a "C", curving the fingers and thumb like a small camera frame.
Hold the "C" hand up at the side of your eye, and raise your non-dominant hand as a flat vertical palm in front of you.
Bring the "C" hand down to touch the flat palm, as if the image you see is captured onto paper.
Keep the flat palm upright and vertical while the "C" hand lands against it.
Keep your gaze and expression neutral; the sign reads as "photo" or "photograph" by context.
tip: Plural of “Photo” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an L, thumb and index finger held open and steady.
Press the palm of the L hand against the palm of your flat non-dominant hand.
Pull the L hand back an inch or two, dip it down an inch or two, then touch the left palm again.
Keep the L hand's palm facing the non-dominant palm through both contacts.
Sign with a firm, even rhythm and a neutral, serious face.
tip: Plural of “Law” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, all fingers curved together into a claw.
Hold your non-dominant forearm or wrist steady in front of you, palm facing down.
Move the C hand in a small circle over the wrist so its thumb brushes the surface.
Keep the base hand flat, palm down, and still while the C hand circles.
Use quick, compact circles in a small signing space like fluent signers do.
tip: Plural of “Computer” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Start both hands above head height, fingertips together, a little off to the side.
Move the hands downward toward a spot in front of your torso.
Change both handshapes into bent V hands while the hands descend.
Land the bent V hands in front of your torso to complete the downward path.
Keep the motion smooth, compact, and neutral-faced.
tip: “Downloading” is signed with the base DOWNLOAD sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

tip: Past form of “Download” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady in front of you.
Place your dominant hand at the near end of the non-dominant hand's top edge.
Move the dominant hand along the top edge until it reaches the far end and falls off.
Keep your palms angled naturally toward each other through the path.
Make the drop-off at the edge quick and decisive, with a matter-of-fact face.
tip: Plural of “End” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your torso, palm facing down.
Curve the hand slightly so it acts like a doorway or barrier.
Sweep your dominant hand under it, entering at the thumb side and exiting at the pinky side.
Let the dominant hand pass through as if a small animal slipping under a wall.
Mouth the English word 'access' while signing — the mouthing is what makes it read as ACCESS rather than ENTER.
tip: “Accesses” is signed with the base ACCESS sign.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G, pinching the thumb against the side of the bent index finger.
Hold the G hand up beside your temple, a few inches out from the side of your head.
Draw one small circle in the air beside your temple with the G hand.
Finish the circle by touching the fingertips of the G hand lightly to your temple.
Angle the G so the fingertips point toward your head; keep your expression calm and neutral.
tip: Plural of “Government” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend both index fingers, folding your other fingers down against your palms.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, with the index fingers pointing forward.
Trace a square in the air, drawing each side with your index fingertips.
Keep the fingertips aimed forward as you outline all four sides of the square.
Keep a neutral expression; the traced outline stands for a board, sign, or billboard.
tip: Plural of “Board” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into hooked X hands, bending the index fingers like small hooks.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the backs of the hands nearly touching.
Twist both wrists in opposite directions, as if wringing out a small cloth.
Let the palms swing toward and then away from each other as the wrists roll.
Keep a neutral expression; the twisting hands picture something becoming different.
tip: “Changes” is signed with the base CHANGE sign.

steps: Shape both hands into flattened O hands, touching each fingertip to its thumb.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, a few inches apart at stomach-to-chest height.
Rotate both wrists forward together, rolling the hands over twice in smooth turns.
Keep both palms angled downward as the hands complete the two forward rolls.
Keep your face relaxed; the rolling motion suggests goods turning over on shelves.
tip: Plural of “Shop” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a flattened O, thumb and fingertips nearly touching.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your torso, palm facing up.
Slap the flattened O hand down onto the flat palm once or twice.
Keep the base palm facing up and steady while the dominant hand taps it.
Finish with a neutral face — the tapping motion carries the meaning.
tip: Plural of “Money” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into V handshapes, index and middle fingers extended.
Hold the V hands up near your eyes, fingertips pointing forward.
Move both hands outward and forward away from your face together.

steps: Hold both hands flat with the fingers together, palms facing each other at chest height.
Move your flat hands apart to show the two opposite walls of the room.
Bend both hands at the knuckles so they form right angles like bent frames.
Bring the bent hands back toward each other to trace the front and back walls.

steps: Hold your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed curved-5 shapes, fingers loosely curled like soft claws.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a W, three fingers up and the thumb holding the pinky.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and horizontal in front of you as the tabletop.

Pat the base hand twice with short downward taps of the dominant hand.

tip: Plural of “Table” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand upright with the fingers together, like a screen edge.
Spread all five fingers of your dominant hand into a 5 handshape.
Press the dominant hand against the edge of the upright hand so it can pivot.
Twist your dominant wrist side to side while it stays pressed to the base hand.

tip: Plural of “Movie” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up in front of you.

steps: Extend your non-dominant hand in front of you in a flat handshape, palm up.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up in front of your chest.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an S handshape, thumb pressed across the curled fingers.

steps: Raise both hands to the sides of your head with your fingers loosely curved and spread.

steps: Close both hands into loose fists with the thumbs resting up on top.

Keep the fist shapes frozen while they travel, as if paving a stretch of road.

steps: Extend your non-dominant hand in front of you, palm facing up with the fingers together.

Keep the non-dominant hand frozen while the dominant hand moves away.

Hold the joined hands a few inches in front of your chest or upper belly.
Push both hands smoothly forward about six inches, away from your body.
Keep both palms angled downward for the whole forward glide.
Hold a steady, determined face — the motion says the action keeps going.
tip: “Continues” is signed with the base CONTINUE sign.

steps: Press your thumbs together with the other fingers tucked into loose fists.
Hold the joined hands a few inches in front of your chest or upper belly.
Push both hands smoothly forward about six inches, away from your body.
Keep both palms angled downward for the whole forward glide.
Hold a steady, determined face — the motion says the action keeps going.
tip: Past form of “Continue” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Close your dominant hand into an S fist, thumb resting across the fingers.
Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Circle the S fist once just above the open palm.
Land the side of the S fist down onto the open palm.
Keep the circle small and smooth, like one turn of the year.
tip: Plural of “Season” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point your non-dominant index finger straight up in front of your chest, like a small post.
Shape your dominant hand into a V, index and middle fingers extended and spread.
Bring the V hand down over the upright finger so the finger rests between the two prongs.
Aim the V fingertips downward as the hand settles onto the finger.
Keep a businesslike, neutral expression — this is the paperwork version of apply.
tip: “Applies” is signed with the base APPLY sign.

steps: Point your non-dominant index finger straight up in front of your chest, like a small post.
Shape your dominant hand into a V, index and middle fingers extended and spread.
Bring the V hand down over the upright finger so the finger rests between the two prongs.
Aim the V fingertips downward as the hand settles onto the finger.
Keep a businesslike, neutral expression — this is the paperwork version of apply.
tip: “Applying” is signed with the base APPLY sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and index finger together into a small pincer, like holding a stamp.
Raise your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest, palm angled sideways.
Tap the pinching hand once against the side of the upright finger.
Angle the pinching hand's palm toward the finger as it taps.
Keep your face neutral — one tap names the machine that prints.
tip: Plural of “Printer” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out in front of you, flat and open with the palm facing down.
Rest the fingertips of your dominant hand on the back of that hand, starting in a flat O handshape.
Slide the dominant hand outward across the back of the base hand while opening it into a spread five handshape.
Repeat the short outward slide a second time — the noun form uses two quick movements.
Keep both palms facing down the whole time, as if laying opinions out on a table for someone.
tip: Plural of “Advice” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl both hands into tight A fists, pressing each thumb firmly against the folded index finger.
Raise your right A fist to your chest and your left A fist to the left side of your abdomen.
Start with both fists hovering about two inches out from your body.
Thump both fists inward against your body twice in a quick in-out-in double motion.
Keep both palms facing toward your body for the entire movement, like gripping a rifle.
Hold a straight, upright posture with a serious, matter-of-fact expression.
tip: Plural of “Military” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed five handshapes, spreading your fingers wide apart.
Hold both hands about an inch in front of your upper chest, thumbs closest to your body.
Brush both hands straight down your chest as if smoothing a shirt, letting the thumbs drag lightly.
Repeat the downward brush a second time in a quick double movement.
Angle your palms slightly toward yourself so the thumbs stay near your chest as they slide.
Keep a neutral expression — actual chest contact is optional; the double brush is what counts.
tip: Plural of “Clothing” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Touch the tip of your dominant index finger to your right temple to begin.
Slide your dominant hand downward while changing the index finger into an "F" handshape.
Raise your non-dominant hand into a matching "F" handshape beside the moving hand.
When both hands reach lower-chest level, drop them sharply downward a few inches and stop dead.
tip: Plural of “Decision” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Bend the middle finger of your dominant hand at the large knuckle so its tip points downward.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with its palm facing up.
Circle the bent middle-finger tip above the upturned palm, then plant the fingertip into its center.
Hold the planted fingertip still for a moment to mark the exact middle point.
tip: Plural of “Middle” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend your dominant hand forward with the fingers together and the palm angled upward.
Curl your fingers inward as if grabbing an invisible object out of the air.
Pull your closed hand back toward your chest in one smooth, decisive motion.
Turn your palm to face your body as the hand arrives near your chest.
tip: “Takings” is signed with the base TAKING sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady in front of you at about waist height.
Bring your dominant hand down an inch or two until it makes contact with the other hand.
Move both hands together downward and outward to the sides in one smooth motion.
End with the hands separated, picturing a whole quantity splitting into parts.
tip: Plural of “Division” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point both index fingers forward so the two fingertips aim toward each other.
Rotate the two index fingers around one another in a small circular motion.
Draw both hands toward your body in one smooth arcing movement.
Keep your palms angled inward toward yourself as the hands arrive near your chest.
tip: “Comings” is signed with the base COMING sign.

steps: Form an "L" handshape with your dominant hand, extending your thumb and index finger.
Place the "L" handshape against your chin with the index finger touching the chin.
Bounce the hand gently on your chin two times while keeping the "L" handshape firm.
Keep your palm angled inward toward your face throughout the two bounces.
tip: Plural of “Lesbian” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into fists and hold them in front of your chest.
Angle the fists toward each other so the knuckles face inward like meshing gears.
Interlock the fingers loosely, then move the hands back and forth in small alternating twists.
Keep the movement compact and rhythmic, as if you are turning a set of gears.
tip: Plural of “Machine” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl both hands into loose fists with each thumb sticking straight up, like signing the number ten.
Hold your non-dominant fist out in front of your chest, thumb up, as the person being followed.
Set your dominant fist a few inches directly behind the non-dominant one, also thumb up.
Move both fists forward together a short distance, keeping the dominant hand trailing behind the other.
Keep both palms facing sideways and your thumbs upright for the whole forward motion.
Look steadily forward as the hands move, as if watching the person ahead of you.
tip: “Follows” is signed with the base FOLLOW sign.

steps: Raise your non-dominant forearm upright in front of your chest, elbow low, like a tree trunk.
Curve your dominant hand into a C, with the thumb and fingers forming a firm half circle.
Rest the wrist of the C hand on top of the upright forearm.
Rock the C hand left and right twice from the wrist, with the same sway as the sign for TREE.
Keep the trunk arm perfectly still so that only the C hand does the moving.
tip: Plural of “Christmas” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Press your dominant thumb against your index fingertip to form a small pinching shape.
Hold the pinched fingers out in front of your chest, facing an imaginary row of options.
Close the fingers onto one option and lift the hand upward and toward your chest.
Angle your palm downward while you draw the selected option inward.
Finish with a small decisive nod of the head, since choosing is an intentional and confident act.
tip: Plural of “Choice” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Cross the middle finger of your dominant hand over its index finger to form an R.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing upward like a paper form.
Lay the R hand down across the fingers of the open palm.
Lift the R, shift it a couple of inches toward the wrist, and set it down again.
Make the double stamp motion with a matter-of-fact expression, as if handling paperwork.
tip: Plural of “Registration” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open your non-dominant hand into a flat five with the fingers together and pointing forward.
Hold that flat hand out in front of your chest with its palm facing sideways.
Cup your dominant hand around the fingertips of the flat hand, catching them from above.
Pull both hands forward together in one firm motion, the dominant hand drawing the other along.
Keep the base hand steady while your dominant hand does the pulling.
Look engaged and forward-facing, the way a leader watches where the group is going.
tip: “Leads” is signed with the base LEAD sign.

steps: Open your non-dominant hand into a flat five with the fingers together and pointing forward.
Hold that flat hand out in front of your chest with its palm facing sideways.
Cup your dominant hand around the fingertips of the flat hand, catching them from above.
Pull both hands forward together in one firm motion, the dominant hand drawing the other along.
Keep the base hand steady while your dominant hand does the pulling.
Look engaged and forward-facing, the way a leader watches where the group is going.
tip: “Leading” is signed with the base LEAD sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Open your non-dominant hand into a flat five with the fingers together and pointing forward.
Hold that flat hand out in front of your chest with its palm facing sideways.
Cup your dominant hand around the fingertips of the flat hand, catching them from above.
Pull both hands forward together in one firm motion, the dominant hand drawing the other along.
