Look engaged and forward-facing, the way a leader watches where the group is going.
tip: Past form of “Lead” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Make an 'I love you' handshape with your dominant hand, extending your thumb, index finger, and pinkie.
Hold the hand in the space in front of your shoulder at about chest height.
Glide the hand forward twice in short, even movements, as if a plane were cruising onward.
Keep your palm facing the floor through the entire movement.
Look in the direction your hand travels with a relaxed, neutral expression.
tip: Plural of “Airport” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up, as your canvas.
Make an 'I' handshape with your dominant hand, extending only your pinkie finger.
Touch the pad of your pinkie to the flat palm and draw a few short strokes, as if sketching with a pencil.
Then add the person marker: hold both flat hands out at your sides with fingers pointing outward.
Sweep both flat hands straight down along your torso, keeping the palms facing each other.
Finish the movement with a slight nod, as if presenting the finished artist.
tip: Plural of “Artist” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an 'F' handshape with your dominant hand, touching your thumb to your index finger and spreading the other three fingers.
Hold the hand out at chest height with the palm facing forward.
Wave the hand from side to side a couple of times using small, tight movements.
Keep the path strictly side to side and never let the hand circle.
Keep a neutral, matter-of-fact expression while signing.
tip: Plural of “Furniture” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form an 'F' handshape with each hand, touching each thumb to its index finger and spreading the other fingers.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the palms facing down toward the floor.
Start with the hands close together near the center of your chest.
Move both hands away from each other in opposite directions in one smooth, even motion.
Keep your palms facing down and your elbows relaxed through the whole movement.
Hold a calm, neutral expression as you finish.
tip: Plural of “Degree” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an 'F' handshape with your dominant hand, touching your thumb to your index finger and spreading the other fingers.
Touch the 'F' hand against your chest or torso where a shirt button would sit.
Arc the hand downward a few inches along your torso.
Touch your torso again to mark the position of a second button.
Repeat once more to show a third button if you want to show several.
Keep a neutral expression and let the taps mark each button's place.
tip: Plural of “Button” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands flat and open, with the fingers extended and together.
Raise both hands to the sides of your head, near your ears or temples.
Move both hands forward together in one short, even motion.
Keep the palms facing each other as the hands travel forward.
Direct your eyes and attention forward, showing concentration on the task.
tip: “Focuses” is signed with the base FOCUS sign.

steps: Form a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers pressed together and the thumb resting along the side.
Bring the hand up to the side of your head, near your cheek or temple.
Rest the side of your head against the hand, tilting slightly as if settling onto a pillow.
Keep the palm facing toward your face with the fingers pointing toward your ear.
Hold the position briefly with a relaxed face, as if you are ready to fall asleep.
tip: Plural of “Bed” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend the middle finger of your dominant hand while the other fingers stay loosely curled.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your chest, palm facing upward like a tray.
Press the middle fingertip into the center of the palm and rock the hand side to side twice.
Keep your dominant palm angled downward as the middle finger pivots in place.
Use a small, relaxed rocking motion — a stiff, wide sweep reads as a different sign.
tip: Plural of “Medicine” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a Y, extending the thumb and pinky while tucking the middle fingers.
Hold the Y handshape beside your head, with the thumb near your ear and the pinky toward your mouth.
Rock the hand with a small double movement, tilting it slightly forward and back twice.
Keep the thumb and pinky extended throughout — folding them in changes the sign entirely.
Keep your face neutral and conversational; TELEPHONE is a plain noun sign.
tip: Plural of “Telephone” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into an E handshape, fingers bent with the thumb tucked beneath them.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your torso, palm facing upward like a tray.
Tap the dominant E hand down onto the non-dominant palm two times, with a short bounce between taps.
Keep the dominant palm facing upward as it lands, so the curled fingers do the tapping.
Hold an assertive, serious expression — this sign presents something as a proven fact.
tip: Plural of “Evidence” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Spread your dominant hand into an open 5-handshape with all fingers extended.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat and horizontal at chest height, palm turned toward your torso.
Draw the dominant hand downward across the flat hand while wiggling all four fingers like falling drops.
Face both palms toward your own torso as the dominant hand slides down.
Do the downward wiggle once or twice depending on the sentence — twice suggests a continuing flow.
tip: Plural of “Blood” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands as flat open hands, fingers together with thumbs alongside.
Hold both hands up in the neutral signing space in front of your shoulders.
Move both hands forward together in one smooth, straight motion.
Keep both palms facing each other, like the two walls of a corridor.
Use one firm forward push and keep your expression neutral throughout.
tip: Plural of “Hall” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like a counter.
Bring your dominant flat hand down to land on it, palm facing down.
Flip the dominant hand over so its back lands on the same palm again.
Make both landings firm and quick using a small wrist flip.
Keep your body relaxed; no extra ROOM sign is needed after this sign.
tip: Plural of “Kitchen” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a hooked two, with the index and middle fingers bent like claws.
Start the hand off to one side of your body at about chest height.
Swing the hand across to the other side in a smooth downward arc.
Keep the palm angled down toward the floor through the whole arc.
Finish with one confident sweep; a single trip from side to side.
tip: “Transfers” is signed with the base TRANSFER sign.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of you with the fingers loosely together.
Rub each thumb against its fingertips in small circles, as if feeling sand or soil.
Keep both hands working side by side at about chest height.
Angle the palms toward your body while the thumbs keep rubbing.
Use a neutral expression and repeat the rubbing two or three times.
tip: Plural of “Ground” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Raise your dominant hand beside your head, forming a loose open hand with the fingers slightly curved.
Bring the hand up to the side of your head, near the top where the hair sits.
Brush the hand downward along the side of your head, as if smoothing a lock of hair.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your head through the whole downward stroke.
Keep your expression neutral, and let the motion stay close to the head instead of floating out wide.
tip: Plural of “Hair” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B handshapes, fingers together and pointing straight up.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the upright fingertips nearly touching at the center.
Move the two hands outward to opposite sides, opening a wide flat span like a wall rising.
Keep the palms facing forward, away from your body, for the whole outward movement.
Hold a neutral expression and keep the hands at chest height; the sign simply depicts the flat surface.
tip: Plural of “Wall” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point both index fingers upward with your other fingers curled into loose fists.
Hold both hands in front of your torso at about chest height.
Twist your wrists as you trace two small upward arcs through the air.
Let each fingertip draw a loose cursive W shape, moving upward and outward.
Keep both palms angled toward each other with the fingers leading the motion.
Pair the sign with a bright, satisfied expression to show a good outcome.
tip: Plural of “Success” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Start with your dominant hand a few inches in front of your chest.
Shape the hand like a loose grip, as if about to unscrew a light bulb.
Move the hand inward until the thumb side approaches your chest.
Close the fingers into a flattened O as the hand reaches your body.
End with the flat of your thumbnail touching your chest, fingertips meeting.
Keep a matter-of-fact expression; this sign claims possession of something.
tip: Plural of “Owner” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form a loose four hand with your dominant hand, fingers together and thumb tucked.
Hold the hand beside your lower cheek, near the chin, palm facing sideways.
Shake the hand downward twice in two small, quick strokes.
Keep the strokes short — about an inch — right against the cheek.
Use a neutral expression; context separates this from the color brown.
Some signers circle a W handshape at the cheek instead — know both, use the common one.
tip: Plural of “Wine” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into loose 5 handshapes with the fingers spread and slightly bent.
Hold both hands up at chest height in front of your body, palms facing each other.
Point the fingertips of each hand toward the fingertips of the other hand, picturing lanes of cars.
Move the hands back and forth past each other in small alternating motions, like vehicles streaming in opposite lanes.
Keep the palms facing each other through the whole alternating movement.
Hold a matter-of-fact expression — the sign simply names the condition of traffic.
tip: Plural of “Traffic” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in flat B handshapes with your thumbs resting alongside your fingers, not forming P shapes.
Raise both hands to the neutral signing space in front of your chest with your palms facing each other.
Move both hands straight downward a few inches together in one smooth, level motion.
Keep both palms facing inward toward each other and both hands moving evenly as they drop.
Keep your expression neutral and avoid any initialized P handshape when you use this sign alone.
tip: Plural of “Agent” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand in an open 5 handshape with all fingers spread in front of you.
Form a flat hand or a relaxed open 5 handshape with your dominant hand beside it.
Tap the thumb of your dominant hand against the tip of the non-dominant thumb, then tap it a second time.
Keep your non-dominant hand still and hold it slightly lower so the two thumb tips can meet.
Use this sign only for a school senior — a senior citizen uses a different established sign.
tip: Plural of “Senior” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form both hands into flattened-O handshapes, with fingertips and thumbs rounded together.
Hold both hands up near your head, starting at about forehead height in front of you.
Push both hands forward away from your head, pull them slightly back, then push forward again in a double movement.
Keep your palms turned slightly inward toward each other as your hands travel outward.
Use the double movement only for the ongoing process of teaching; one quick movement means the verb teach.
tip: Plural of “Teaching” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat in a B handshape and keep your non-dominant hand flat and still beside it.
Raise your dominant hand to chest height in front of you, starting with the palm facing forward.
Swing your dominant hand outward as if opening a door, then swing it back inward to close it, using two movements.
Keep your palm facing forward the whole time and let your pinkie-side edge act as the door's hinge.
Keep your face neutral; depending on context this same sign can also mean closet, cupboard, or cabinet.
tip: Plural of “Door” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in front of you with your index fingers extended straight and pointing upward.
Curl both index fingers into X handshapes as you begin moving both hands downward together.
Draw the path of a question mark in the air with your moving hands, then open both into palm-down 5 hands to dot it.
Keep your palms facing downward as the 5 handshapes finish the sign in the neutral signing space.
Maintain a thoughtful, inquisitive expression while the hands trace the question-mark shape.
tip: Plural of “Testing” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form both hands into F handshapes by touching each thumb to its index fingertip.
Hold both F hands in front of you about eight inches apart at mid-chest height.
Move your right hand up a few inches while your left hand moves down the same distance at the same time.
Reverse the motion, bringing the right hand down as the left hand rises, like a balance scale tipping.
Hold your right palm facing left and your left palm facing right, and keep your expression serious and formal.
tip: Plural of “Trial” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hook your dominant index finger over your thumb to form an X handshape, folding the remaining fingers down.
Place the hooked X hand just under your chin, close to the front of your throat.
Flick the X hand forward about three inches with a quick wrist motion, then repeat the flick once more.
Angle your palm slightly downward so the hooked X points forward as it slides away from your throat.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — this sign simply names the material.
tip: Plural of “Metal” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Spread the fingers of both hands wide into open five handshapes.
Raise both hands to chest height in front of you, with all the fingers pointing upward.
Push the hands together so the fingertips interlock, like two opposing scrimmage lines clashing at the snap.
Ram the hands together twice in a quick double movement, keeping the fingers meshed.
Keep the palms facing each other through both rams of the sign.
Hold a neutral, game-ready expression — the double clash is part of the sign.
tip: Plural of “Football” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curve the fingers of both hands into loose bent handshapes, with the fingertips pointing downward.
Raise both bent hands to the tops of your shoulders, close to your neck.
Touch the fingertips down onto your shoulders, then lift and touch again with a firm double tap.
Keep the palms angled inward toward your chest through both contacts.
Hold a steady, earnest expression — the repeated tap marks this as a duty.
tip: Plural of “Responsibility” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your torso in loosely clawed shapes, fingers curved with the dominant hand just above the other.
Let the two hands hover near each other, with the upper hand's palm angled slightly downward toward the lower one.
Shift both hands a few inches outward to the sides at the same time.
As the hands move apart, close each hand into a firm S fist, thumb resting over the curled fingers.
Hold a calm, sincere expression, as if resting steady confidence on the other person.
tip: “Trusts” is signed with the base TRUST sign.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your torso in loosely clawed shapes, fingers curved with the dominant hand just above the other.
Let the two hands hover near each other, with the upper hand's palm angled slightly downward toward the lower one.
Shift both hands a few inches outward to the sides at the same time.
As the hands move apart, close each hand into a firm S fist, thumb resting over the curled fingers.
Hold a calm, sincere expression, as if resting steady confidence on the other person.
tip: “Trusting” is signed with the base TRUST sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your torso in loosely clawed shapes, fingers curved with the dominant hand just above the other.
Let the two hands hover near each other, with the upper hand's palm angled slightly downward toward the lower one.
Shift both hands a few inches outward to the sides at the same time.
As the hands move apart, close each hand into a firm S fist, thumb resting over the curled fingers.
Hold a calm, sincere expression, as if resting steady confidence on the other person.
tip: Past form of “Trust” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of your torso with all fingers and thumbs spread loosely apart.
Bring the hands toward each other at chest height until the fingertips of both hands meet in the middle.
Tap the fingertips of both hands together once, as if many people are gathering into one group.
Angle the palms toward each other and slightly downward as the fingertips touch.
Keep a neutral, informative expression instead of the raised-eyebrow look of a question.
tip: Plural of “Session” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Relax both hands into open 5 handshapes, fingers together and slightly loose, with the thumbs ready.
Hold both hands at chest height with the thumbs aimed at your upper chest.
Poke your upper chest twice with both thumb tips, moving the hands forward and back with each poke.
Angle both palms inward toward your body so the thumbs can reach the chest squarely.
Keep your face relaxed and easy, matching the carefree time-off feeling.
tip: Plural of “Vacation” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form a C handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingers curved open.
Hold the C in front of your body at chest height, slightly to your dominant side.
Trace a quick small circle with the C hand, moving clockwise from your own point of view.
Keep the hand upright with the opening of the C facing outward toward your audience as you circle.
Mouth the word 'century' while signing, since viewers usually need the sentence context to catch it.
tip: Plural of “Century” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a loose A fist, keeping the thumb sticking up and slightly out.
Rest that fist on the open palm of your flat non-dominant hand, held at about waist height.
Lift both hands upward together a few inches, as if boosting the fist from below.
Keep the non-dominant palm facing up so it visibly supports the raised fist.
Aim the sign toward the person you mean: start near yourself for 'I help you', near them for 'you help me'.
tip: Plural of “Assistance” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Flatten both hands with fingers together and thumbs tucked, palms facing the ground.
Raise the flat hands to about waist height, keeping them low in front of your body.
Touch the fingertips of the two hands together in the center to form one level plane.
Sweep both hands smoothly outward to the sides, spreading them wide like laying a surface.
Follow the sweep with your eyes and keep a neutral face, letting the wide flat motion carry the meaning.
tip: Plural of “Floor” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a firm O and hold it upright at chest height.
Spread the fingers of your dominant hand, then bend the middle finger sharply at its largest knuckle.
Poke the bent middle finger into the opening of the non-dominant O hand.
Pull the finger back out and immediately slap your open dominant palm down over the O opening.
Make both the poke and the slap quick and snappy, since the sudden snap sells the fizzy idea.
tip: Plural of “Pop” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and fingers loosely together, as if gripping a thin matchstick.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat before your chest with the palm facing sideways and fingers up.
Strike the dominant fingertips downward across the base palm, like scratching a match to light it.
For the noun form, make two very small quick strikes instead of one sweeping stroke.
For the verb form, use one single large strike and keep your expression focused.
tip: “Matches” is signed with the base MATCH sign.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and fingers loosely together, as if gripping a thin matchstick.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat before your chest with the palm facing sideways and fingers up.
Strike the dominant fingertips downward across the base palm, like scratching a match to light it.
For the noun form, make two very small quick strikes instead of one sweeping stroke.
For the verb form, use one single large strike and keep your expression focused.

steps: Point your dominant index finger forward, other fingers tucked away.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, as your paper.
